name: Fulvestrant (Faslodex)

lead: Fulvestrant is a prescription injection that blocks and breaks down the estrogen receptor, approved for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It is sometimes named in hormone discussions as a pure estrogen blocker, with a possible flatter male chest as the goal.

It binds the estrogen receptor and marks it for destruction, reducing estrogen signaling in breast tissue. Published research covers cancer and rare pediatric conditions, and no study addresses appearance.

paras: It is given as a clinician-administered intramuscular injection under medical care.
Reported effects include injection-site reactions, nausea, weakness, raised liver enzymes and clots. The label warns about bleeding risk, hepatic impairment and fetal harm. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Fulvestrant is an injectable pure antiestrogen that occasionally comes up for gynecomastia: degrading estrogen receptors reduces estrogen signaling in breast tissue, which could mean a flatter chest. It is used for breast cancer, and no study addresses appearance.

lead: Fulvestrant, sold as Faslodex and as generics, is an antiestrogen given by intramuscular injection. It is the first selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) approved for medical use and is used for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women [1][2].

It is a pure estrogen-receptor antagonist rather than a partial agonist like tamoxifen, which is why it is sometimes mentioned in muscle and hormone-related discussions as a 'pure' estrogen blocker. The sources reviewed describe only oncology and a few rare-disease uses; no study of fulvestrant for appearance goals was found.

Large randomized trials have tested it mainly in combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors and other targeted agents in advanced breast cancer [3][4]. The US label lists injection-site reactions, bleeding risk, hepatic impairment and embryo-fetal toxicity among its warnings [2].

paras: Fulvestrant is used for HR-positive metastatic or locally advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women, alone or with agents such as palbociclib, abemaciclib or ribociclib [1][2]. A 2017 Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found it about as safe and effective as other endocrine therapies used first or second line [1]. It has also been tried for peripheral precocious puberty in girls with McCune-Albright syndrome [1].
No encyclopedia, trial or regulatory source reviewed describes fulvestrant as a treatment for appearance concerns. Its injectable-only route and prescription status are noted in the sources [1][2].

Wikipedia lists nausea, injection-site reactions, weakness and raised liver transaminases as very common, with venous thromboembolism, hot flushes, headache and back pain among common effects [1]. The label's most frequent reactions were injection-site pain, nausea, bone pain, arthralgia, headache, back pain and fatigue, and warnings cover bleeding risk, hepatic impairment, injection-site reaction and embryo-fetal toxicity [2].

Fulvestrant binds the estrogen receptor, blocks its action and makes the receptor unstable so the cell degrades it, hence the term SERD [1][5]. Wikipedia adds that it can falsely elevate estradiol readings on some blood immunoassays because of its structural similarity to estrogen [1].

After intramuscular injection absorption is slow, with peak levels around 5 days and an elimination half-life of roughly 40 to 50 days; it is about 99% protein bound and eliminated largely in feces [1].

Phase 3 trials of palbociclib plus fulvestrant (PALOMA-3), abemaciclib plus fulvestrant (MONARCH 2) and ribociclib plus fulvestrant (MONALEESA-3) reported improved progression-free survival in advanced HR-positive breast cancer, with overall-survival benefits reported for palbociclib and abemaciclib combinations [3][4][6][7][8]. Capivasertib with fulvestrant and alpelisib with fulvestrant have also been tested in randomized trials [9][10]. A phase 2 trial of 30 girls with McCune-Albright syndrome examined fulvestrant for precocious puberty [11]. All of this concerns cancer or pediatric endocrine disease; no trial of fulvestrant for appearance-related purposes was found.

Fulvestrant was found through rational drug design and developed by AstraZeneca. It was approved in the US in 2002 and the EU in 2004, and was the first SERD approved [1]. A generic version has since been FDA approved [1]. In 2011 the UK's NICE concluded that it had not been shown to be significantly better than existing treatments [1].
Because fulvestrant cannot be taken orally, newer oral SERDs such as elacestrant have been developed, and prodrug approaches are under study [1].

timeline.event: Fulvestrant approved in the United States [1].
UK NICE finds no evidence of significant advantage over existing treatments [1].
